topStories.headline: Sixty Unused Tiny Cabins Sit Locked in a Bayview Parking Lot While Neighbors Sleep on the Sidewalk
topStories.dek: A $7 million shelter investment has sat empty for nearly a year at Jerrold Commons — and city officials have not explained why.
topStories.body:
For close to a year, sixty tiny shelter cabins have sat shuttered in a Bayview parking lot at Jerrold Commons on Jerrold Avenue, their doors closed and windows dark, even as a small encampment of tents and cardboard lines the sidewalk a block away. The SF Standard reported on September 2 that city officials have offered no public explanation for why the cabins remain out of use, despite Mayor Daniel Lurie's repeated pledges to reduce homelessness and clean up city streets.

The cabins were purchased during the Breed administration for more than $100,000 apiece and originally opened in 2024 on a Mission District lot as a temporary bridge to more stable housing. When that site was cleared for an affordable housing project, the plan had been to relocate the cabins to a SoMa location — but that deal collapsed, and the mayor's office redirected the units to Jerrold Commons strictly for storage. The abrupt decision drew immediate criticism from District 10 Supervisor Shamann Walton, who said he was not notified and that the move violated agreements made with the Board of Supervisors.

The irony is visible to anyone who walks the block. Jerrold Commons already operates a functioning cabin community for older adults on one side of a green construction fence — a program the city has called a model success. The 60 additional cabins sit unused on the other side. According to a Mission Local analysis cited in Hoodline's coverage, as of April 2026 the city had opened 863 new shelter beds under Lurie but closed enough older sites that the net gain was just 403 beds, with scheduled future closures expected to shrink that figure to 303 by 2028.

District 10 has long carried a disproportionate share of the city's shelter and transitional-housing siting. Walton, who terms out in November, has accused the mayor of a bait-and-switch on shelter policy and of treating the Bayview as a default destination for services rejected elsewhere. Neither the Department of Homelessness and Supportive Housing nor the mayor's office had publicly explained the delay as of the Standard's September 2 publication.

topStories.headline: Bayview Oyster Bar Is Opening This Month on Third Street
topStories.dek: April Spears, the Bayview native behind the beloved Auntie April's, is debuting a new seafood restaurant at 5114 Third St. as part of a city-funded wave of nine new businesses on the corridor.
topStories.body:
Bayview Oyster Bar is opening this month at 5114 Third St., the storefront that sat dark since Word. A Cafe closed in 2021 when the pandemic ended foot traffic on the block. Owner April Spears, who grew up in the Bayview and previously ran Auntie April's — a fried chicken and waffles institution for 15 years — is blending Northern California seafood with her Louisiana roots. The space will hold about 25 dining seats, a raw bar at the front, a seafood counter, and eventually a backyard patio, with historic photographs of the Bayview on the walls. The menu will center on Dungeness crab, king salmon and oysters, with some seafood prepared over open flames in a style inspired by New Orleans cooking, the SF Chronicle reported in August.

The restaurant is one of nine new Bayview businesses receiving support through the Office of Economic and Workforce Development's Storefront Opportunity Grants program, an initiative from Mayor Lurie that has allocated $3 million citywide to fill vacant commercial spaces. The nine Bayview recipients together received $800,000 — second only to downtown in the city's total grant investment. Grants range from $50,000 to $100,000 and can cover tenant improvements, equipment, inventory and permits.

Seven of the nine new Bayview businesses are food-and-drink operations, including Panamanian fusion spot Properly Seasoned Kitchen, Ethiopian fast-casual Moya Bayview, and smoked-meat specialist Phatwood Smokehouse Deli. The Chronicle noted that from 2019 to 2025 the Bayview saw a 31 percent decline in sales-tax revenue — making this cohort of openings a significant test of whether targeted public investment can rekindle a commercial corridor that has struggled since the pandemic.

topStories.headline: India Basin Waterfront Park Is Open for Programming — Grand Celebration Scheduled for October 19
topStories.dek: The 900 Innes site is running weekly events and community programs while final shoreline construction continues next door, with a neighborhood-wide grand opening set for next month.
topStories.body:
The India Basin Waterfront Park at 900 Innes Avenue in Bayview–Hunters Point is open and running community programming this fall. According to SF Recreation and Parks, the site now includes two new public piers, a floating dock, ADA-compliant access to the Bay Trail, public restrooms, a food pavilion and a makers' shop supporting boat-building programs — amenities the waterfront neighborhood had long lacked. The Welcome Center is open Wednesday through Sunday, 10 a.m. to 3 p.m., with rotating food vendors and an Artist in Residence program.

A grand opening celebration is scheduled for Saturday, October 19, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. at the 900 Innes site, per the Rec and Parks events calendar. The event will feature live music, cultural performances, free food, historical tours, and on-site connections to workforce training and community grant programs tied to the park's Equitable Development Plan.

Construction continues on the third and final phase of the project — the renovation of the adjacent India Basin Shoreline Park — which will connect to the 900 Innes parcel to form a continuous 10-acre waterfront park. Rec and Parks lists that phase as running through approximately early 2028, with crews currently completing earthwork and shoreline stabilization. The full project is a $200 million partnership among the SF Recreation and Park Department, Trust for Public Land, San Francisco Foundation, A. Philip Randolph Institute, and the Bayview–Hunters Point community, and is one of only a handful of parks in the nation guided by a community-written Equitable Development Plan.

moreNews.headline: SCRAP Opens Permanent Bayview Home at 141 Industrial Street
moreNews.body: SCRAP — the Scroungers' Center for Reusable Art Parts, a nonprofit store of donated art materials co-founded by Ruth Asawa — held its grand reopening in mid-August at a permanent new location at 141 Industrial St. in the Bayview, the SF Standard reported on August 14. The organization purchased the Bayview property after SFUSD decided to demolish its previous building to construct a central kitchen; property records cited by the Standard show the purchase price was approximately $5.3 million. The new space is larger than any prior home and will host community workshops in bookmaking, printmaking and other art forms, while continuing to partner with local schools and supply teachers with materials at little or no cost.

moreNews.headline: Bayview Street Repaving Underway; Excelsior and Portola Work to Start in November
moreNews.body: A multi-phase street repaving program got underway in the Bayview in July, with 24 blocks expected to be resurfaced by March 2028, the SF Standard reported on April 22. The largest section of the project — 50 blocks covering the Portola and Excelsior — is scheduled to begin in November and run through summer 2028. The city builds its annual repaving priority list around traffic volume, transit routes, bike lanes, and the opportunity to bundle underground utility repairs into the same street closure. All work is funded with state dollars announced by Mayor Lurie's office.
